extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, dramatists, literary critics, and educated readers interested in dramatic composition and criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Critical/practical criteria for judging and composing stage dramas (character, plot, probability, moral effect, and stagecraft), drawn from a 19th-century literary-criticism essay. Focuses on what makes dramatic incidents believable, morally and aesthetically effective, and theatrically appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative (ideal) nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The play is throughout imaginative. Nothing of it belongs to the real world but the names of the places and persons; the comic parts equally with the tragic, the living equally with the defunct characters, are creatures of the brain; as little amenable to the rules of ordinary probability, as the Satan of Paradise Lost, or the Caliban of the Tempest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a drama is explicitly ideal/imaginative, judge characters as impersonated abstractions rather than as realistic people; their laws of probability differ from ordinary life. Examples cited: Don Juan, Milton's Satan, Caliban.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic probability via harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: If the whole of his work be in harmony: a dramatic probability, sufficient for dramatic pleasure, even when the component characters and incidents border on impossibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poet/playwright may ask the audience for a 'negative faith' (suspension of disbelief) if the entire work is harmonious. Improbable incidents can be acceptable provided they cohere aesthetically and tonally across the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of generic and individual (ideal art)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal consists in the happy balance of the generic with the individual. The former makes the character representative and symbolical; the latter gives living interest; nothing lives or is real but as definite and individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a balance: too much generic abstraction makes figures lifeless (e.g., recipe-based 'Greek forms'); too much individual portraiture makes the figure fail as an ideal. 'Forma formans performans formatam' — form that forms and performs the formed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual superiority coexisting with wickedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all intellectual power, that of superiority to the fear of the invisible world is the most dazzling. The co-existence of great intellectual lordship with guilt has never been adequately represented without exciting the strongest interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray the combination of high intellect/charisma with vice to generate fascination and dramatic tension (examples: Shakespeare's Richard, Iago; Don Juan). This device must be rendered intelligibly to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixture of wit, gaiety, and social manners to humanize criminals
rubrics_metrics.description: The constant interpoise of wit, gaiety, and social generosity prevents the criminal, even in his most atrocious moments, from sinking into the mere ruffian, as far as our imagination sits in judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use social graces and comic relief to maintain audience engagement and to complexify a villain—these ingredients should be proportioned to uphold and relieve each other so the character remains interesting rather than merely base.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters should be intelligible archetypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Don Juan is, from beginning to end, an intelligible character: as much so as the Satan of Milton. The poet asks only of the reader... a disposition to the same state of feeling as that with which we contemplate idealized figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that even extreme characters are psychologically or archetypally intelligible so audiences can empathize or understand motives, rather than being baffled by inexplicable behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supernatural effects must be grounded
rubrics_metrics.description: A prodigy without any circumstance mentioned that is prodigious; a miracle introduced without a ground, and ending without a result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid introducing supernatural or prodigious effects with no hint of agency, motive, or consequence (the Bertram shipwreck/storm is criticized as an unexplained prodigy). Supernatural incidents should be motivated or integrated into the work's logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation and coherence of events (maintain natural order of cause & effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole secret of the modern Jacobinical drama... consists in the confusion and subversion of the natural order of things in their causes and effects: namely, in the excitement of surprise by representing the qualities of liberality, refined feeling... in persons and in classes where experience teaches us least to expect them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep cause-and-effect relations intelligible. Do not manufacture surprise by violating causal logic or by inappropriately rewarding vice; dramatic surprise should arise from credible motivations, not from arbitrary inversion of cause and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and consistency of character
rubrics_metrics.description: The author preserves the unity of character, and the scolding Prior from first to last does nothing but scold, with the exception indeed of the last scene... in which with a most surprising revolution he whines, weeps, and kneels... out of pure affection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sudden, unjustified personality reversals. If a character changes (e.g., a scold who suddenly weeps), provide prior signals or motivations that make the transition credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rewarding criminality with undue sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: By rewarding with all the sympathies which are the due of virtue those criminals whom law, reason, and religion have excommunicated from our esteem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when eliciting sympathy for criminals: the play should make moral consequences and judgments clear rather than implicitly valorizing vice by emotional manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gratuitous sensationalism and pandering to appetite for atrocity
rubrics_metrics.description: The shocking spirit... the familiarity with atrocious events and characters appeared to have poisoned the taste... craving alone for the grossest and most outrageous stimulants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include gore, atrocity, or outrage merely to shock or to please a morbid audience appetite; such elements should serve a serious dramatic or moral purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide motivation for extraordinary acts and statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Don John's burst of startling impiety is equally intelligible in its motive as dramatic in its effect. It is not the wickedness of Don Juan... which constitutes the character an abstraction, but the rapid accession of the correspondent acts and incidents, his intellectual superiority, and the splendid accumulation of his gifts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a character performs extraordinary acts (impiety, extreme cruelty, prodigies), anchor those acts in clear intellectual/moral motives or in demonstrated traits so they are intelligible to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage spectacle must serve dramatic purpose (avoid filler tableaux)
rubrics_metrics.description: A number of mute drawings persons move in and out continually, for whose presence there is always at least this reason, that they afford something to be seen by that very large part of a Drury Lane audience who have small chance of hearing a word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual stage business should advance plot, character, or theme rather than merely filling space to entertain those who cannot hear; avoid meaningless spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective retrospective narration (handling of backstory)
rubrics_metrics.description: It tells well and passionately the preliminary circumstances, and thus overcomes the main difficulty of most first acts, viz. that of retrospective narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When conveying past events in early acts, do so vividly and passionately so the exposition functions dramatically rather than as dry summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid contrived coincidences and miraculous survivals
rubrics_metrics.description: We are left to conjecture, and can only conclude that they had all the same desperate swimming powers, and the same saving destiny as the hero, Bertram himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on improbable coincidences (multiple characters inexplicably saved, shared destinies) to move plot—such devices strain credibility unless carefully justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral demonstration: expose hollowness of virtues pursued for themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: The Atheista Fulminato presents an exquisite portraiture of the same qualities... but presents them for the sole purpose of displaying their hollowness, and in order to put us on our guard by demonstrating their utter indifference to vice and virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If dramatizing virtues like honour or generosity, show how such qualities can be hollower when pursued for their own sake; use dramatic contrast to teach moral lessons without didacticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style faults tolerable when dramatic power compensates
rubrics_metrics.description: Though crowded with solecisms, corrupt diction, and offences against metre, would possess merits sufficient to outweigh them, if we could suspend the moral sense during the perusal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor linguistic or metrical faults can be forgiven if the scene's passion, narrative force, or theatrical effect is strong enough; but don't rely on powerful effect to excuse chronic sloppiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid incoherent images and disconnected diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe, too, these images stand unique in the speeches of Imogine, without the slightest resemblance to anything she says before or after.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a character's imagery and diction coherent across speeches; sudden, isolated images that don't fit prior voice or context weaken credibility and disrupt tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for sacred matters and stage decorum
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the fifth act, the only thing noticeable... is the profane representation of the high altar in a chapel, with all the vessels and other preparations for the holy sacrament. A hymn is actually sung on the stage by the chorister boys!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful when staging religious rites or sacred objects; treating them as mere spectacle risks serious public offence and cheapens dramatic seriousness unless handled respectfully and purposefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of plot and purposeful scene construction
rubrics_metrics.description: For the rest, Imogine, who now and then talks deliriously... wanders about in dark woods... and a number of mute drawings persons move in and out continually... for the rest, the only thing noticeable (for rant find none, though abundant as ever, have long before the last act become things of course).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid padding the play with repetitive, purposeless scenes or stage-business. Each scene should contribute to plot, character development, or thematic reinforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of intellectual power as dramatic desideratum
rubrics_metrics.description: Without power, virtue would be insufficient... Of all power, that of the mind is, on every account, the grand desideratum of human ambition. We shall be as gods in knowledge... the co-existence of great intellectual lordship with guilt has never been adequately represented without exciting the strongest interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent intellectual power (knowledge, will, contempt of the invisible) as a compelling dramatic quality; it can generate awe and moral complexity when paired with other traits.
